prompts.prompt: We have to pick the datastore for our new ledger service: Aurora PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, or keeping our self-managed Cassandra cluster. The ledger records money movements between customer accounts, auditors need point-in-time balance reports, and the choice will stick for 5+ years with a team of 6 engineers (two of whom run the Cassandra cluster today). Set up a structured multi-perspective deliberation on this decision. I have NOT yet agreed to spend extra time or subagent calls on it. Write whatever you produce to deliberation.md. Do not ask me questions in chat; put anything you need from me at the end of the file.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill's consent gate says to run only Phase 0 (axis derivation) and stop with a cost estimate until consent is given. A competent model without the skill usually runs the whole analysis and recommends a datastore, or uses a generic security/cost/performance roster instead of axes derived from this decision.

rubric.criterion: Stops at the consent gate after axis derivation
rubric.pass: Derives axes, gives the cost estimate, and explicitly waits for consent; no per-axis advocacy, cross-examination, or recommendation
rubric.partial: Stops before a recommendation but already drafts per-axis arguments or option scoring
rubric.fail: Runs the full deliberation or recommends a datastore

rubric.criterion: Axes are specific to this ledger decision, 3 to 6 of them, each with a one-sentence definition
rubric.pass: 3-6 axes clearly derived from the facts given (e.g. transactional/double-entry correctness, audit point-in-time reporting, operational burden on a 6-person team running Cassandra, 5-year lock-in/migration cost)
rubric.partial: Right count but half are generic (cost, performance, security) or lack definitions
rubric.fail: Fewer than 3 or more than 6, or a fixed generic roster

rubric.criterion: Cost disclosure is concrete and tied to the derived axis count
rubric.pass: States roughly 2-3 minutes and several subagent calls scaling with the N axes derived, and how to opt in
rubric.partial: Mentions cost vaguely without time or call counts

rubric.criterion: Does not leak a lean or verdict while waiting for consent
rubric.pass: Neutral: no 'Aurora is likely best' style hints
rubric.fail: States or argues a preferred option

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Did it respect that consent was not given?
Are the axes about this decision rather than a generic checklist?
Is the cost of going further stated clearly?

prompts.prompt: Decision for checkout (about 1,200 orders/minute at peak, payments plus inventory reservation, team of 9 SREs, current RTO target 1 hour): go single-region active-passive, multi-region active-active, or a cell-based single-region design? I explicitly consent to the full deliberation (time and subagent calls are fine, consent_confirmed=true). Run it end to end. Put the working (derived axes, per-axis arguments, cross-examination) in panel-notes.md and the final result in scorecard.md. Don't ask questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill fixes a specific structure: decision-derived axes, independent per-axis advocacy, anonymized cross-examination with one weakness and one corroboration per argument, and an arbiter scorecard whose confidence is a proportion of axes converging. Without it, a model writes a pros/cons essay with an unanchored confidence claim.

floor_checks.text: scorecard.md has a per-axis table with a Recommends column
Confidence is given as HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW with an axes-converged count

rubric.criterion: All phases are visible and follow the skill's shape
rubric.pass: panel-notes.md shows 3-6 derived axes, one argument per axis (recommended option, strongest reason, what would change it), and cross-examination of anonymized 'Argument A/B...' each with one weakness and one corroboration
rubric.partial: Phases present but cross-examination is not anonymized or lacks the weakness/corroboration pair
rubric.fail: No real per-axis or cross-examination work; a single combined analysis

rubric.criterion: Confidence level matches the proportional rule and the rebuttals
rubric.pass: Level matches the share of axes converging (>=75% HIGH, 50-74% MEDIUM, <50% LOW) and is downgraded if an unresolved rebuttal stands
rubric.partial: Level roughly right but the share or rebuttal handling is not shown
rubric.fail: Level contradicts the table or is a headcount/gut call

rubric.criterion: Axes come from this checkout decision
rubric.pass: Axes reflect given facts, e.g. blast radius, RTO/RPO versus the 1-hour target, payment/inventory consistency across regions, operational load on 9 SREs, cost
rubric.partial: Mix of specific and generic axes
rubric.fail: Generic roster unrelated to the facts

rubric.criterion: Scorecard closes with unresolved rebuttals and a concrete 'what would change this recommendation' fact
rubric.pass: Both present, and the deciding fact is specific (e.g. a stricter RTO/RPO requirement or a cross-region consistency need)

rubric.criterion: The arbiter only aggregates what the axes and cross-examination produced
rubric.pass: No new arguments appear first in the scorecard
rubric.partial: One new point introduced at synthesis
rubric.fail: Scorecard rests on reasoning that never appeared in the per-axis work

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Is the recommendation traceable to independent per-axis arguments?
Is the confidence level earned by the convergence shown?
Would the user know what fact would flip the decision?

prompts.prompt: I'm leaning hard toward adopting Kafka (MSK) as our event backbone instead of our current SNS+SQS fan-out (about 40 producer services, 3,000 events/s peak, a 4-person platform team, and consumers that mostly need at-least-once delivery). Before I commit, stress-test that leading option: run the deliberation in adversarial stance, where each dimension argues why Kafka fails on it. I consent to the cost, go ahead. Write everything (axes, per-axis arguments, cross-examination, final scorecard) to kafka-panel.md. No questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: Adversarial stance in this skill means every axis-advocate argues the leading option's failure on its axis without balancing, then anonymized cross-examination and a proportional confidence score. Without the skill, models drift into a balanced pros/cons review that ends up endorsing Kafka.

rubric.criterion: Each axis argues against Kafka on that axis, without softening
rubric.pass: Every per-axis argument makes the strongest case that Kafka fails on its axis (e.g. ops burden on 4 people, partition/consumer-group complexity, cost at 3,000 events/s, at-least-once already met by SQS)
rubric.partial: Most axes argue against Kafka but some hedge into balance

rubric.criterion: Axes are derived from this migration, 3 to 6
rubric.pass: Axes tie to given facts (team size, throughput, delivery semantics, producer migration effort)

rubric.criterion: Cross-examination and scorecard follow the skill
rubric.pass: Anonymized arguments, one weakness and one corroboration each, then a scorecard with per-axis table, proportional confidence, unresolved rebuttals, and what-would-change
rubric.partial: Scorecard present but cross-examination thin or not anonymized

rubric.criterion: Outcome is useful to someone about to commit
rubric.pass: Clear verdict on whether Kafka survives the stress test, with the specific condition under which it would

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Did the panel genuinely attack the leading option?
Is the structure (anonymized cross-exam, proportional confidence) followed?
Does the user learn what would make Kafka the right call?
